Esau said to Jacob, “Give me some of your cooked food to eat, because I am very tired.” Because of this, he was named Edom.
Jacob said to Esau, “Give me your birthright.”
Esau said, “Look, I am about to die. What use is being the firstborn to me?”
Jacob said to him, “Swear to me today that you will transfer your birthright to me.” Esau swore to him and transferred his birthright to Jacob.
Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew. He ate and drank, got up, and went away.
There was another famine in the land, besides the famine that had occurred in Abraham’s time. Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in Gerar.
The Lord God appeared to him and said, “Do not go down to Egypt. Stay in the land that I tell you.”
“Stay in this land, and I will go with you and bless you, for I will give this land to you and your descendants. I will fulfill with you the oath I swore to your father Abraham.
I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven, and I will give all this land to your descendants. Through your descendants all the nations of the earth will be blessed,
because Abraham listened to my voice and kept my commandments, my ordinances, and my laws.”
Isaac stayed in Gerar.

The men of the land asked Isaac about Rebekah, his wife. He told them, “She is my sister,” because he was afraid to let them know that she was his wife, lest the men of that land kill him because of Rebekah, his wife, for she was beautiful.
He stayed there a long time. When the king looked out through a window, he saw Isaac playing affectionately with Rebekah, his wife.
Abimelech summoned Isaac and said to him, “Surely she is your wife, yet you told me, ‘She is my sister.’” Isaac said, “Because I thought, ‘They might kill me because of her.’”
Abimelech said to him, “What is this you have done to us? One of my relatives might easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought sin upon me without my knowing it.”
He commanded all his people, saying to them, “Anyone who harms this man will be sentenced to a terrible death.”
Isaac sowed in that land and received a hundredfold yield. The Lord God blessed him.
The man prospered and grew greater and greater, until he was very great.
He acquired sheep, cattle, and many fields, and the Philistines envied him.
The Philistines blocked up all the wells that Abraham’s men had dug in the days of Isaac’s father, and filled them with earth.
Abimelech said to Isaac, “Go away from us, for you have become much stronger than we are.”
Isaac went away from there, camped in the valley of Gerar, and stayed there.

Isaac again dug the wells of water that the servants of his father Abraham had dug, which the Philistines had filled in after his father Abraham died. He gave them the names that Abraham had given them.
Isaac’s servants dug wells in the valley of Gerar and found a spring of fresh water.
Isaac’s herdsmen and the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled, and they said, “The water is ours.” He named that well the Well of Injustice, because they had treated him unjustly.
Isaac moved away from there and dug another well there. They opposed him over it, and he named it Hatred.
He moved away from there and dug a well, and they did not quarrel with him over it. He named it Rehoboth, saying, “For now the Lord has made room for us and increased our numbers in our land.”
He moved from there to Beersheba.

The Lord God appeared to him that night and said to him, “[?] I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid. I am with you, and I will bless you and make your descendants numerous for the sake of your father Abraham.”
He built an altar there to the Lord his God and called on the name of the Lord his God. He planted a garden there, and Isaac’s men dug a well there.
Abimelech came to him from Gerar with Ahuzzath, the overseer of his shepherds, and Phicol, the commander of his army.
Isaac said, “Why have you come to me after hating me and driving me away from you?”
They said to him, “When we saw that the Lord God was with you, we said, ‘Let there be an oath between you and us, and let us swear to one another.’”
“So that you will do us no harm, for we did not mistreat you, but treated you well and sent you away in peace. And now you are blessed by the Lord God.”
He made an oath to them, and they ate and drank.
They rose in the morning and swore oaths to one another. Isaac sent them away, and they went in peace.
That same day Isaac’s servants arrived and told him about the well they had dug. They had found no water in it.
He named it Oath. For this reason the name of that town is Oath to this day.
When Esau was forty years old, he took as his wife Judith, the daughter of Baal the Hittite, and Basemath, the daughter of Elon the Hittite.
They were at odds with Isaac and Rebekah.
When Isaac had grown old, [?], and his eyes had grown dim so that he could not see, he called Esau, his older son.
He said to him, “Look, I have grown old, and I do not know the day of my death.”
“Now take your hunting equipment, your sling and your bow, and go out into the field and hunt for me.
Prepare food for me the way I like it, and bring it to me to eat, so that I may bless you before I die.”
Rebekah heard Isaac saying this to his son Esau. Esau went out into the field to hunt for his father.
Rebekah said to Jacob, her younger son, “Listen, I heard your father saying to your brother Esau,
‘Bring me some of what you hunt and prepare food for me, and I will bless you before the Lord before I die.’
Now, my son, obey me and do as I tell you.
Go to our flock and bring me two fine firstborn young goats. I will prepare them as food for your father, the way he likes it.
You will take it to your father, and he will eat and bless you before he dies.”
Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, “Look, my brother Esau is hairy, but I am not hairy.”
“My father might feel me, and I would seem to him like someone mocking him. I would bring a curse upon myself, not a blessing.”
His mother said to him, “Let your curse fall on me, my son. Only obey me: go and bring me what I told you.”
He went and brought it to his mother, and she prepared food for his father just as he liked it.
Rebekah took the fine clothes of her older son Esau, which she had with her, and dressed her younger son Jacob in them.
She also put the skins of the two young goats on his arms and neck.
She put the food and the bread she had prepared into the hands of her son Jacob.
He went in to his father and said, “Father!” His father said to him, “Here I am. Who are you, my son?”
Jacob said to him, “I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done what you told me. Get up, sit down, and eat some of what I have hunted for you, so that your soul may bless me.”
Isaac said to his son, “How did you find it so quickly, my son?” He said to him, “The Lord your God put it before me.”
Isaac said to him, “Come near so that I can feel you, my son, to find out whether you really are Esau or not.”
Jacob came near to his father Isaac, and he felt him. Isaac said, “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s.”
He did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like Esau’s hands, and Isaac blessed him.
He said to him, “Are you my son Esau?”
He said to him, “Bring me some of what you hunted, my son, so that I may eat and bless you.” He brought it to him, and he ate. He brought him wine, and he drank.
Isaac said to him, “Come close and kiss me, my son.”
He came near and kissed him. He smelled him and smelled the scent of his clothes, and said, “Look, the scent of my son is truly like the scent of a field that the Lord has blessed.”
He said to him, “May God give you the dew of heaven and the dew of the earth, and multiply your grain and wine.”
May nations serve you, and may angels bow down to you. Be lord over your brother, and may your father's sons bow down to you. May whoever blesses you be blessed, and whoever curses you be cursed.
After Isaac had finished blessing his son Jacob, and Jacob had gone out from the presence of his father Isaac, Esau came back from hunting.
He too prepared food and brought it to his father. He said to him, “Get up, Father, and eat some of what your son has hunted for you, so that you may bless me with all your soul.”
He said to him, “Who are you?” Esau said to him, “I am your firstborn son, Esau.”
Isaac trembled very violently and said to him, “Who, then, brought me what he had hunted? I ate it and blessed him, and he is blessed.”
When Esau heard his father’s words, he cried out loudly and with great bitterness, and said, “Bless me too, Father!”
He said to him, “Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing.”

Esau said, “He is rightly named Jacob, for he has cheated me, and today is the second time! He took my birthright, and now today he has taken my blessing.” Esau said to him, “Father, have you not kept a blessing for me too, Father?”
Isaac answered Esau, “I have made him your master, and I have made all his brothers his servants. I have given him abundant wine and grain. What can I do for you, my son?”
Esau said to his father Isaac, “Do you have only one blessing, Father?” Then Esau cried out and wept.
Isaac said, “Look, your livelihood shall come from the dew of heaven above and from the dew of the earth.
Live by your sword, and you shall serve your brother. But if you wish, you shall throw his burden off your neck.”
Esau continually hated Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. Esau said in his heart, “Let the days of mourning for my father draw near, so that I may kill my brother Jacob.”
Rebekah was told what her older son had said. She sent for her younger son Jacob and said to him, “Look, your brother Esau is hunting you and wants to kill you.
Now, my son, listen to what I tell you. Get up and go to Mesopotamia, to my brother Laban in Haran.
Stay with him for a few days, until your brother’s anger cools
and he forgets what you did to him. Then I will send for you and bring you back from there, so that you two will not both perish in one day.”
Rebekah said to Isaac, “I hate my life because of the daughters of Canaan. If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of this land, why should I go on living?”
Isaac called his son Jacob, blessed him, and said to him, “Do not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.
Arise and go to Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel, your mother's father, and take a wife for yourself from the daughters of Laban, your mother's brother.
May my God himself go with you, make you great, bless you, and multiply you, so that you become many nations.
May he give the blessing of your father Abraham to you and to your descendants after you, so that you may inherit the land he gave to Abraham.”
Isaac sent his son Jacob to Syrian Mesopotamia, to Laban, the son of Bethuel the Syrian and the brother of Rebekah.

When Esau saw that his father had blessed Jacob and that he had gone to Syrian Mesopotamia to take a wife from there, and that, when blessing him, his father had commanded him not to take a wife from there, from the daughters of Canaan,
and that Jacob had obeyed his father and mother and gone to Mesopotamia,
When Esau saw that the daughters of Canaan were displeasing to his father Isaac,
he went to Ishmael and took Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham’s son and Nahor’s brother, to be his wife in addition to his other wives.
Jacob set out for Beersheba and went to Haran.
[He came to a place] and spent the night there, because the sun had set. He took a stone from that place, put it under his head, and spent the night there.
He dreamed and saw a ladder (of gold) on the earth, with its top reaching heaven. The angels of God were ascending and descending on it.

The Lord stood above it and said to him, “I am the Lord, the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac your father. Do not be afraid. This land on which you are lying I will give to you and your descendants.

Your descendants will be like the sand of the earth. Your descendants will multiply and spread to the west, the south, the north, and the east. All the nations of the earth will be blessed through you and through your descendants.
I will go with you and protect you wherever you go. I will bring you back to this land, and I will not leave you until I have done for you everything I have told you.”
Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, “The Lord is in this place, and I did not know it!”
He was afraid and said, “How awe-inspiring this place is! Here is the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”
Jacob rose in the morning, took the stone he had put under his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil on its top.
He named that place the House of God. Previously, the place had been called Ulamhsa.
Jacob made a vow, saying, “If the Lord God is with me and protects me on this journey I am making, and gives me food to eat and clothes to wear,
And bring me back safely to my father's house, and the Lord will be my God.
then this stone that I have set up will be a house of God for me, and of everything he gives me I will surely give you a tenth.”
Jacob arose and went east to Laban, the son of Bethuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau.
He looked and saw a well in the open country, and there were three sheep resting beside it, for they watered the sheep from that well. A large stone lay over the mouth of the well.
All the shepherds would gather there and roll the stone away from the mouth of the well. Then they would water their sheep and put the stone back over the mouth of the well.
Jacob said to them, “My brothers, where are you from?” They said to him, “We are from Haran.”
He said to them, “Do you know Laban, the son of Nahor?” They said to him, “We know him.”
He said to them, “Is he well?” They said to him, “He is well.” As they were speaking this way, Rachel came with her father’s sheep.
He said to them, “The time has not yet come for your livestock to be gathered. Water them and let them go and graze.”
They said to him, “We cannot until all the shepherds gather and roll this stone away from the mouth of the well. Then we can water our sheep.”
While they were saying this, Rachel arrived with her father’s sheep.
When Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of Laban, his mother’s brother, [he rolled the stone away from the well and watered her sheep for her.]
Jacob kissed Rachel, cried out aloud, and wept.
He told Rachel that he was the son of her father’s sister and that he was Rebekah’s son. Rachel ran and told her father this news.
When Laban heard the name of Jacob, the son of his sister Rebekah, he ran to meet him, embraced him, kissed him, and brought him into his house. Jacob told Laban everything that had happened.
Laban said to Jacob, “You are of my own bone and flesh.” Jacob stayed with him for thirty days.
Laban said to Jacob, “Because you are my relative, should you serve me for nothing? [Tell me] what your wages will be.”
Laban had two daughters. The older one was named Leah, and the younger one Rachel.
Leah’s eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in appearance and lovely in face.
Jacob loved Rachel, and Jacob said to Laban, “I will serve you for seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter. (Give her to me to be my wife.)”
Laban said to him, “It is better for me to give her to you (my kinsman and my own flesh) than to another man. Stay, then.”
Jacob served for seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him like only a few days because he loved her.
Jacob said to Laban, “Now give me my wife so that I may sleep with her, for I have completed my time of service.”
Laban gathered all the people of the place and held a feast.
When evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob.
Laban gave his daughter Leah the girl Zilpah to be her servant.
When morning came, there was Leah! Jacob said to Laban, “What have you done to me? Was it not for Rachel that I served you? Why have you mocked me?”
Laban said to him, “That is not how it is done in our country. They do not give the younger daughter first while the older one is still there.”
“Complete seven years for this one too, and I will give you the other one as well in return for serving me another seven years.”
Jacob did the same for her too and completed her seven years. Then Laban gave Rachel to Jacob.
He gave Bilhah to Rachel to be her maidservant.
Jacob slept with Rachel and loved her more than Leah. He served Laban another seven years for her.
When the Lord saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.
Leah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Reuben, saying, “The Lord has seen my affliction, and now my husband will love me.”
Leah conceived again and gave birth to another son for Jacob. She said, “The Lord has heard that I am hated, and he has given me this one too.” She named him Simeon.
She conceived again and gave birth to a son. She said, “Now my husband will be with me, because I have borne him three sons.” She named him Levi.
She conceived again and bore a son, and said, “Now, once again, I will give thanks to the Lord God for this.” Therefore she named him Judah. And she stopped bearing children.
When Rachel saw that she was not bearing children for Jacob, she became jealous of her sister Leah. She said to Jacob, “Give me children, or I will die.”
Jacob became angry with Rachel and said to her, “Am I like God to you, who has withheld the fruit of your womb from you?”
Rachel said to him, “Here is my servant Bilhah. Go and sleep with her, and let her give birth on my knees, so that I too may have children through her.”
She gave him Bilhah to be his wife, and Jacob slept with her.
Bilhah conceived and gave birth to a son for Jacob.
Rachel said, “God has given judgment in my favor, heard my voice, and given me a son.” Therefore she named him Dan.
Bilhah, Rachel’s servant, conceived again and bore a second son for Jacob.
She said, “God has delivered me, and I have matched my sister and prevailed over her.” She named him Naphtali.
When Leah saw that she was not bearing children and had stopped giving birth, she took Zilpah, her maidservant, and gave her to Jacob to be his wife.
Zilpah became pregnant by Jacob and bore a son.
Leah said, “I too have been blessed,” and she named him Gad.
Zilpah became pregnant again and gave birth for Jacob.
Leah said, “I am blessed, and women will call me blessed,” and she named him Asher.
Reuben went out during the wheat harvest and found mandrakes in the countryside. He brought them to his mother. Rachel said to Leah, “Give me your son’s mandrakes.”

Leah said, “Is it not enough that you have taken my husband from me? Do you also want to take my son’s mandrakes from me?” Rachel said to Leah, “Not so. Let him spend tonight with you in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.” (And she gave them to her.)

Jacob came in from the field toward evening, and Leah met him (toward evening) and said to him, “You will spend the night with me today, for I have bought you with my son's mandrakes.” And he spent that night with her.
God listened to Leah, and she became pregnant and bore his fifth son.
Leah said, “God has given me my wages because I gave her my son’s mandrakes.” She named him Issachar, meaning “wages.”
Leah became pregnant [again] and bore Jacob a sixth son.
Leah said, “God has given a good judgment in my favor. From today onward, then, my husband will love me, because I have borne him six sons.” She named him Zebulun.
After this she bore a daughter and named her Dinah.
God remembered Rachel and opened her womb.
She became pregnant and bore Jacob a son. She said, “God has taken away my disgrace.”
She named him Joseph and said, “May God give me another son.”
When Rachel had given birth to Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, “Send me away so that I may go to my homeland and my own country.”
“Give me my children and my wives, for whom I served you. You yourself know how I have served you.”
Laban said to him, “If I have found favor in your sight—for I know that God has blessed me because of you—
“Specify the wages I am to give you.”
Jacob said to him, “Do you not know how I have served you, and how many of your animals are in my care?”
For I found them few in number, but they have increased and multiplied, and the Lord has blessed them wherever I have set foot. And now, when will I provide a household for myself?
Laban said to him, “What shall I give you?” Jacob said to him, “You need not give me anything. If you do this for me, I will again graze your sheep and look after them.
“Let all your sheep pass by today, and separate from them every sheep whose fleece is white, and every one that is white or speckled in color and appearance. These will be my wages.
“Every one that is not speckled and is not white in appearance will be yours.”
Laban said to him, “Let it be as you have said.”

That day he separated the mottled [sheep], the speckled ones, and the white ones, and all the mottled goats, the speckled ones, the white ones, and those that were red in color. He gave them to his sons.
He put a three-day journey between them and Jacob, while Jacob grazed the sheep that remained to Laban.
Jacob took a green branch of storax and a large branch of [?]. Jacob peeled them, stripping off their green bark and exposing the white of the branches he had peeled.

He placed these branches in the watering troughs so that, when the sheep came to drink, the branches would be before them. When the sheep came to drink, they would conceive while looking at the branches.
When they came and drank, they conceived while looking at the branches, and the sheep gave birth to white, earth-colored, and speckled young.
Jacob separated the males of his flock and placed them before the white rams and those marked with white. He set his own flock apart and did not mix them with Laban’s sheep.
Then, at the times when the sheep conceived, Jacob would place those rods before the sheep in the troughs, so that they would conceive while looking at those rods.
After the sheep had given birth, he no longer put the branches there. All those with markings belonged to Jacob, and those without markings belonged to Laban.
Jacob became exceedingly wealthy and acquired many livestock, cattle, male and female servants, camels, and donkeys.
Jacob heard what Laban’s sons were saying: “Jacob has taken all our father’s possessions, and from our father’s possessions he has acquired all this wealth.”
Jacob saw that Laban’s expression toward him was not as it had been before.
The Lord God said to Jacob, “Return to your father’s land and to your relatives, and I will be with you.”
Jacob called Leah and Rachel into the field where the flock was.
He said to them, “Look, I see from your father's face that he is not disposed toward me as he was before, but the God of my father is with me.”
“You know that I have served your father with all my strength.
But your father has mistreated me and changed my wages of ten sheep. Yet the Lord did not allow him to harm me.

If he said to me, ‘The multicolored ones will be your wages,’ all the sheep gave birth to multicolored young. If he said to me, ‘The white ones will be your wages,’ they all gave birth to white young.
The Lord took all your father’s sheep and gave them to me.
Then, at the time when the animals conceived, I saw with my own eyes in a dream that the male sheep and goats mounting the goats and sheep were white, multicolored, earth-colored, and speckled.
The angel of the Lord said to me in the dream, ‘Jacob, Jacob!’ I said, ‘Here I am. What is it?’

He said to me, ‘Look with your own eyes and see: the male goats and sheep mounting the goats and sheep are white, multicolored, earth-colored, and speckled, because I have seen everything Laban is doing to you.

I am the Lord your God, who appeared to you in the land of the Lord, where you anointed a pillar for me and made a vow to me. Now get up and go to the land where you were born, and I will be with you.’”
They answered him, “Do we still have any inheritance in our father’s house?
Does he not treat us as strangers? He sold us and consumed the price paid for us.”
All the wealth that God has taken from our father's house belongs to us and our children. Now do everything that God has told you.
Jacob got up, took his wives and children, and put them on camels.
He took all his possessions, the goods he had acquired in Mesopotamia, and everything that belonged to him, and went to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan.
Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole her father’s gods.
Jacob kept it secret from Laban the Syrian and did not tell him that he was leaving.
He departed with everything that belonged to him, crossed the river, and stayed in Gilead.
And Laban the Syrian was told that Jacob had left.
Laban took all his relatives with him and pursued them for a seven-day journey, and he overtook them in the hill country of Gilead.
God came to Laban the Syrian in a dream at night and said to him, “Be careful not to speak harshly against Jacob.”
Laban overtook Jacob. Jacob was pitching his tent on the mountain, and Laban stationed his relatives in the hill country of Gilead.
Laban said to Jacob, “What have I done in secret, that you should wrong me and steal my daughters away like captives taken in war?”
“If you had told me, I would have sent you away with joy and gladness, with singing, drums, and lyres.
Why was I not allowed to kiss my children and my daughters? Now you have acted like a fool.
Even now I could do you harm, but the God of your father said to me last night, ‘Be careful not to do harm to Jacob.’
Now go, since you wanted to go to your father’s house. But why did you steal my gods?”
Jacob answered Laban and said to him, “Because I thought you would take your daughters and all my possessions away from me by force.”

Now look to see whether any of your belongings are with me, and take them. Laban went in but found nothing at all. Jacob said, “Whoever you find your gods with shall not live. Here, in the presence of these relatives of ours.” Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them.
Laban entered Leah’s tent but found nothing. He went out and entered Jacob’s tent and searched it. He entered the tent of his two concubines but found nothing, and then he entered Rachel’s tent.
Rachel had taken her father’s gods, put them inside the camel’s saddle, and sat on it.

She said to her father, “Do not think that I am showing you disrespect, my lord, because I cannot rise before you, for I am menstruating.” Laban searched Rachel’s entire tent but did not find his gods.
Jacob became angry and argued with Laban, saying to him, “What is my offense, and what is my sin, that you have pursued me?
You have searched all my possessions. What have you found from the belongings of your own house? Let us put it before these relatives of ours, and let them judge between us.
For twenty years I have tended your sheep and goats, and they did not miscarry. I did not eat a sheep from your flock.
I did not bring you an animal eaten by wild beasts; I paid for it myself, from my own possessions. If anything was stolen, whether by day or by night, I paid for it.
I spent the night in the dew, and sleep fled from my eyes.
As of today, I have spent twenty years serving you in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your sheep, and you set my wages at ten sheep.
Had the God of my father Abraham not been with me, and had it not been for the Fear of Isaac, you would have sent me away with nothing. God saw the toil of my hands and rebuked you last night.”

Laban answered Jacob and said to him, “The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, and the livestock are my livestock. Everything you see is mine. But what can I do today to these daughters of mine, or to the children they have borne?
Now come, let us swear an oath, you and I, and let there be peace between me and you.”
Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.

Jacob said to his relatives, “Gather stones.” They gathered stones and made a heap, and they ate and drank beside that heap of stones. Laban said to him, “This stone is a witness between me and you today.”
Laban called it “Heap of Witness,” and Jacob called it the same.
Laban said to Jacob, “Look, this pillar that I set up is a witness between me and you.” For this reason its name was called “Heap of Witness.”
And the vision that the Lord showed me: may he watch between me and you, because we are separated from one another.
You must not mistreat my daughters or take another wife besides them.
And look, there is no one here with us.
If I do not cross over to you, may this heap and this pillar pursue me with harm; and likewise you, if you do not cross over to me.
May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor judge between us. And Jacob swore to him by the Fear of his father Isaac.
Jacob offered a sacrifice on the mountain and called his relatives. They ate and drank and spent the night on that mountain.
Laban rose in the morning, kissed his daughters and his children, and blessed them. Then Laban turned back toward his own country and departed.
Jacob continued on his way. Jacob looked with his eyes and saw the army of God encamped, and the angels of God met him.
When Jacob saw them, he said, “This is the camp of God.” And he named that place “Camp.”
Jacob sent messengers to his brother Esau in the region of Seir, in the land of Edom.
He instructed them and said, “Say this to my lord Esau: ‘Your servant Jacob says this: I lived with Laban and have stayed there until today.
I have acquired donkeys, camels, cattle, sheep, male servants, and female servants. I have sent word to my lord Esau so that I, your servant, may find favor with you.’”
The messengers whom Jacob had sent returned to him and said, “We went to your brother Esau, and now he is coming to meet you, with four hundred men accompanying him.”
Jacob was very afraid and did not know what to do. He divided the people with him, along with the sheep and cattle, into two camps.
Jacob said, “If Esau comes to one camp and destroys it, the other camp will escape.”
Jacob said, “God of my fathers, God of Abraham and God of Isaac, the Lord who said to me, ‘Go to the country where you were born, and I will do good to you’—
may he then do good to me, with all the righteousness and uprightness you have shown me, your servant. For I crossed this Jordan with my staff, and now I have become two camps.
Save me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I fear him for my own life, lest he come and kill me, and kill the mother together with her children.
You said to me, ‘I will do good to you, and I will make your descendants like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted because it is so plentiful.’”
He spent that night there and brought out a gift to be taken to his brother Esau.
Two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams;
thirty female camels with their young, forty heifers and ten bulls, twenty donkeys and ten foals.
He entrusted them to his servants, each herd separately, and said to them, “Go ahead, and leave a distance between one herd and the next.”
He said to the first, “If you meet my brother Esau and he asks you, ‘Whose is this? Where are you going? And whose is what is going ahead of you?’”
Tell him, “It belongs to your servant Jacob. It is a gift he has sent to his lord Esau, and he himself is following behind us.”
He instructed the first, the second, the third, and all those who went ahead of him driving the herds, saying to them, “Say this to my brother Esau if you meet him.

Tell him, ‘Look, your servant Jacob is coming behind us.’” For he said, “I will be safe from him through this gift that they are carrying ahead of him. Then I will see his face, so that he may welcome me peacefully.”
Then he sent the gift on ahead, while he spent that night in the camp.
He got up and took his two wives, his two concubines, and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them across the stream and brought all his possessions across.
Jacob remained alone, and a man wrestled with him until dawn.
When he saw that he could not overcome him, he took hold of the sinew of his thigh while wrestling with him.
He said to him, “Let me go, for dawn has broken.” But he replied, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”
He said to him, “What is your name?” He answered, “Jacob.”
He said to him, “Your name will no longer be Jacob; instead, your name will be Israel, because you have prevailed with God and with human beings.”
He said to him, “Tell me your name.” But he replied, “Why do you ask my name?” And he blessed him there.
Jacob named that place “Vision of God,” for he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life has been saved (and my face).”
The sun rose as he left “Vision of God,” and his leg was making him limp [?].

For this reason, to this day the children of Israel do not eat the sinew that made him limp, which is in the hollow of the thigh, because he took hold of the sinew of Jacob’s thigh (that sinew of the thigh).
Jacob looked and saw his brother Esau coming, with four hundred men accompanying him. Jacob divided his children among Leah, Rachel, and his two concubines.
He placed his concubines with their children in front, Leah and her children behind them, and Rachel with Joseph behind her.
He himself went ahead of them and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother.
Esau ran ahead to meet him, embraced him around the neck, and kissed him, and they both wept.
When he looked and saw both his wives and their children, he said to him, “Who are these to you?” He replied, “They are my children, whom God has graciously given your servant.”
His concubines came with their children and bowed down.
Leah came with her children and bowed down. Afterward Rachel came with Joseph and bowed down.
He said to him, “What do you mean by this whole company that I encountered?” Jacob said to Esau, “I did this for you, my lord, so that I might find favor in your sight.”
Esau said, “I have plenty, my brother. Keep what is yours.”
Jacob said to him, “If I have found favor in your sight, accept my gift from my hand, because seeing your face is like seeing the face of God.”
“And if you love me, accept the gift I have brought you, because God has been gracious to me, and I have everything.” He urged him, and he accepted it.
Esau said to him, “Get up, and let us go onward.”

Jacob said to him, “You yourself know, my lord, that the children are weak, and that the sheep and cattle in my care are nursing their young. If we drive them hard for one day, [?], all our animals will die.”

“Go ahead of your servant, my lord. We will travel as we are able, for we spend the day on the road as we travel; and whenever we travel, we will go at the children’s pace, until we reach our lord in Seir.”
Esau said to him, “Let me leave some of the people who are with me.” But he replied, “Why do that? It is enough for me that I have found favor in your sight, my lord.”
That day Esau went back on his way to Seir.
Jacob stayed in the camp and made an enclosure there for himself and his animals. For this reason he named that place “Dwelling.”
Jacob arrived at Salem, in the city of Shechem, which is in the hill country of Canaan, when he came from the rivers of Syria. He arrived opposite the city.
He took a plot of land and pitched his dwelling there. He bought the field from Hamor, Shechem’s father, for a hundred sheep.
He set up an altar there and called upon the God of Israel there.
Dinah, Leah’s daughter, whom she had borne to Jacob, went out to see the daughters of that land.
Shechem, the son of Hamor the Horite, the ruler of the land, saw her. He took her, lay with her, and dishonored her.
He looked upon the soul of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, and loved the young woman, and spoke about her [?].
Shechem said to his father Hamor, “Get this young woman for me, so that she may be my wife.”
Jacob heard that the son of Hamor had defiled his daughter Dinah. His sons were in the field with the livestock, and Jacob kept silent until they arrived.
Hamor, Shechem’s father, came to Jacob to speak with him.

His sons came from the field, and when they heard, they were deeply shocked and grieved, because Shechem had done a disgraceful thing against Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter. Such a thing was not lawful.
He spoke to them and said, “My son Shechem loves your daughter. Give her to him to be his wife.
Intermarry with us: give us your daughters, and take our daughters for your sons.
Live with us. Look, the land is spacious before you. Settle in it and work it.”
Shechem said to her father and her brothers, “I have found favor in your sight, and I will give whatever you say.
(Set this requirement for me before you, and whatever you say.) However greatly you increase her bride-price, I will give it to you. Give me this girl to be my wife.”
Jacob’s sons answered Shechem and his father Hamor deceitfully, and spoke to them because they had defiled their sister Dinah.
Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, said to them, “We cannot do this thing, giving our sister to an uncircumcised man, because that would be a disgrace to us.
Only on this condition will you become like us and we live with you: if you circumcise all your males.
We will give you our daughters and take your daughters as our wives. We will live with you and become one people.
But if you do not listen to us, we will take our daughters and leave.”
These words pleased Hamor and Shechem.
The young man did not delay in doing this thing, because he loved Jacob’s daughter. He was more honored than anyone else in his father’s household.
Hamor and Shechem went to the place opposite the city and spoke to all the men of their city.

They said to them, “These men are friendly toward us. Let them live in our land and work it, for the land is spacious before them. Let us take their daughters as our wives and give them our daughters.
Only in this must we become like them, so that these men too may become like us and we may become one people: let us circumcise every male among us, just as they are circumcised.
Will not their flocks, their possessions, and their livestock be ours? Only let us become like them in this, and let them live among us.”
All who entered the city gate said yes to Hamor and his son Shechem. Every male among them was circumcised in the foreskin of his own flesh.
Then, on the third day, while they were in pain and wounded, the two sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, each took his own sword, boldly entered the city, and killed its males.
They also killed Hamor and Shechem, took their sister Dinah, and brought her out of Shechem's house.
Jacob's sons came to the slain and plundered the city in which their sister Dinah had been defiled.
They took their sheep, cattle, and donkeys, and everything that was in the fields and in the city.
They also took their inhabitants, their wives, and all their belongings captive, and plundered everything in the city and in the houses.

Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, “You have brought trouble on me and made me hated by everyone living throughout the land, among the Canaanites and Perizzites. I am few in number, and they will gather against me and kill me. I and my household will be destroyed.”
They said to him, "Why, then, did they treat our sister like a prostitute?"
God said to Jacob, "Get up, go to Bethel, and live there. Build an altar there to God, who appeared to you when you were fleeing from your brother Esau."
Jacob said to his household and to everyone with him, "Remove these foreign gods from among you, take off your clothes, and change your clothes.
Get up, and let us go up to Bethel and build an altar there to God, who heard me on the day of my distress, who was with me, saved me on my journey, and brought me through."
They gave Jacob all the foreign gods and everything they had with them, as well as the earrings in their ears. Jacob hid them in the tree at Shechem and destroyed them, until today, to this very day.
Israel departed from Shechem, and the fear of God fell upon the cities around them, so they did not pursue the sons of Israel.
Jacob arrived at Luz, which is in the land of Canaan.
He built an altar there and named that place Bethel, because God had appeared to him there when he fled from his brother Esau.
Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died and was buried below Bethel, by the oak of weeping.
God appeared to Jacob when he came out of Mesopotamia in Syria, and God blessed him.
He said to him, "Your name shall not be Jacob, but Israel."
He said to him, "I am your God. Multiply and become numerous. Nations and an assembly of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come from you.
The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give this land to your descendants after you."
God went up from him, from the place where God had spoken to him.
Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he had spoken to him. He poured a drink offering over it and poured oil over it.
Jacob named that place Bethel.
He departed from Bethel and pitched his tent by the tower of Eder. Then, as he drew near the land of Ephrathah, approaching Ephrathah, Rachel gave birth and suffered in childbirth.
Then, while she was in the pain of childbirth, her midwife said to her, "Believe me, this too will be a son for you."
Then, as her life was about to leave her—for she was dying—she named him “Son of my suffering,” but his father named him Benjamin.
Rachel died and was buried on the road to Ephrathah, which is Bethlehem.
Jacob set up a pillar over her grave, and it has been called the pillar of Rachel's grave to this day.
Then, while Israel was living in the land, Reuben went and slept with Bilhah, the concubine of his father Jacob. Israel heard of it, and it was evil in his eyes. Jacob's sons were twelve.
The sons of Leah: Reuben, his firstborn, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
The sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant: Dan and Naphtali.
The sons of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant: Gad and Asher.
The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Syrian Mesopotamia.
Jacob came to his father Isaac in the town of Mamre, in the plain—that is, Hebron—in the land of Canaan, where Abraham and Isaac had lived.
Isaac lived for one hundred and eighty years.
He died in old age and was gathered to his relatives, old and having completed his days. His sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
This is the genealogy of Esau, who is Edom.
He took wives for himself from the daughters of Canaan: Adah, daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, son of Zibeon the Hivite;
and Basemath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.
Adah bore him Eliphaz, and Basemath bore him Reuel.
Oholibamah bore him Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are Esau’s sons who were born to him in the land of Canaan.

Esau took his sons, his wives, everyone living in his household, all his livestock, and all the possessions he had acquired in the land of Canaan. Esau left the land of Canaan, moving away from his brother Jacob.
For their possessions were numerous, and they could not live together because of their many possessions.
Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau himself is Edom.
This is the genealogy of Esau, the father of Edom, in the hill country of Seir.
These are the names of Esau’s sons: Eliphaz, son of Adah, Esau’s wife, and Reuel, son of Basemath, Esau’s wife.
The sons of Eliphaz, Esau’s son, were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.
Timna, the concubine of Eliphaz, Esau’s son, bore him Amalek. These are the descendants of Adah, Esau’s wife.
The sons of Reuel, Esau’s son: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the descendants of Basemath, Esau’s wife.
These are the sons of Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and wife of Esau, whom she bore to Esau: Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.
These are the chiefs among Esau’s sons. The sons of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn: Chief Teman, Chief Omar, Chief Zepho, and Chief Kenaz;
Chief Korah, Chief Gatam, and Chief Amalek. These are the chiefs descended from Eliphaz in the land of Edom, who were descended from Adah.

These are the chiefs among the sons of Reuel, Esau’s son: Chief Nahath, Chief Zerah, Chief Shammah, and Chief Mizzah. These are the chiefs descended from Reuel in the land of Edom, who were descended from Basemath, Esau’s wife.
These are the chiefs among the sons of Oholibamah, Esau’s wife: Chief Jeush, Chief Jalam, and Chief Korah.
These are Esau’s sons, the chiefs of Edom.
These are the sons of Seir the Horite who lived in the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, and Anah;
And Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These are also the Horite chiefs, the sons of Seir.
These are the sons of Lotan: Hori and Heman. Lotan's sister was Timna.
The sons of Shobal were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.
These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who found Jamin in the wilderness while the donkeys of his father Zibeon were grazing.
These are the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah.
These are the sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan.
These, then, are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
These are the Horite chiefs: Chief Lotan, Chief Shobal, Chief Zibeon, and Chief Anah;
Chief Dishon, Chief Ezer, and Chief Dishan. These are the Horite chiefs, according to their chieftainships, in the land of Seir.
These are the kings who reigned in Edom before a king reigned over Israel.
Balak son of Beor reigned in Edom, and the name of his city was Dinhabah.
Balak died, and Jobab son of Zerah, from Bozrah, reigned in his place.
Jobab died, and Husham, from the land of the Temanites, reigned in his place.
Husham died, and Hadad son of Bedad, who defeated the Midianites in the fields of Moab, reigned in his place. The name of his city was Avith.
Hadad died, and Samlah, from Masrekah, reigned in his place.
Samlah died, and Saul, from Rehoboth on the river, reigned in his place.
Saul died, and Baal-hanan son of Achbor reigned in his place.
Baal-hanan son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his place. The name of his city was Phogu, and the name of his wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab.
These are the names of Esau's chiefs, according to their clans, their regions, and their names: Chief Timna, Chief Alvah, Chief Jetheth;
Chief Oholibamah, Chief Elah, Chief Pinon;
Chief Kenaz, Chief Teman, Chief Mibzar;
Chief Magdiel, Chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, according to their dwelling places in their land. Esau himself is the father of Edom.
Jacob lived in the land where his father had lived, in the land of Canaan.

This is the lineage of Jacob. Joseph was seventeen years old and tended his father's sheep with his brothers. He was a young man among the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father's wives. They brought an evil accusation against Joseph to his father Israel.
Jacob loved Joseph more than all his sons because he had fathered him in his old age, and he made him a robe of many colors.
When his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak a kind word to him.
Joseph had a dream and told it to his brothers.
He said to them, “Listen to this dream that I have dreamed.”
“I saw your sheaves, each belonging to one of you, in the middle of the field. My sheaf rose and stood upright, and your sheaves turned and bowed down to my sheaf.”
They said to him, “Are you really going to reign over us? Will you indeed become our master?” And they hated him still more because of his dream and his words.
Again he had another dream and told it to his father. He said to him, “Look, I have dreamed another dream, and this was the dream: the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.”
His father rebuked him and said to him, “What is this dream you have dreamed? [?] Will I, your mother, and your brothers come and bow down to the ground before you?”
His brothers were jealous of him, but their father kept this matter in his heart.
His brothers went to pasture their sheep in Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, “Aren’t your brothers in Shechem? Come, let me send you to them.” He said to him, “Yes, here I am.”
He said to him, “Go and see whether your brothers and their sheep are well, and bring me word.” He sent him from the valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.
A man found him wandering about in the open country. He asked him, “Whom are you looking for?”
Joseph said to him, “Tell me where my brothers are pasturing their sheep.”
The man said to him, “They have moved on from here, but I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’” Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
They saw him from a distance, before he came near them, and plotted to kill him.
They said to one another, “Here is that dreamer!”
“Come, let us kill him and throw him into one of these pits. We will say, ‘A wild beast ate him,’ and we will see what becomes of his dreams.”
When Reuben saw him, he rescued him from their hands and said to them, “Do not take his life.”
“Do not shed his blood. Put him into one of these pits in the wilderness, but do not lay your hands on him.” This was so that he could rescue him from their hands and return him to his father.
Then, when Joseph reached them, they stripped him of the ornate robe he was wearing.
They took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was new and had no water in it.

They sat down to eat food. When they looked up, they saw a merchant coming from Gilead. He was an Ishmaelite, and their camels were loaded with spices, resin, and liquid storax, which they were taking down to the land of Egypt.
Judah said to his brothers, “What will we gain if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?”
“Come, let us sell him to these Ishmaelites, and let us not lay our hands on him, for he is our brother and our own flesh.” His brothers listened to what he told them.

As those Ishmaelites were passing by, they sold him to them. His brothers pulled Joseph up and brought him out of the pit, and they sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty dinars. They took Joseph to the land of Egypt.
Reuben returned to the pit, and when he did not find him, he tore his clothes.
He returned to his brothers and said to them, “The boy is not in the pit! Where am I to go now?”
They took his fine linen robe, slaughtered a young goat over it, and soaked his robe with blood.
They took it to their father and said to him, “We found this (blood). Look and see whether it is your son’s garment or not.”
He recognized it and said, “It is my son’s garment. A wild beast has eaten him; a beast has torn Joseph apart.”
Jacob tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, tied it around his waist, and mourned his son for many days.

His sons and daughters gathered and came to comfort their father and relieve his grief. But he refused to be comforted and said, “Instead, I will go down to my son in the grave, mourning him.” And his father wept.
The Ishmaelites sold Joseph in the land of Egypt to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s chief cook.
Then, in those days, Judah went down away from his brothers and stayed with an Adullamite named Hirah.
He saw the daughter of a Canaanite man. Her name was Shua, and he took her and married her.
She conceived and bore a son, and she named him Er.
She conceived again and bore a son, and she named him Onan.
Once again she bore a son, and they named him Shelah. She was in a place called Chezib when she bore them.
Judah took a wife named Tamar for Er, his firstborn son.
Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked before the Lord, and the Lord killed him.
Judah said to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife, fulfill your duty as her brother-in-law, and raise up offspring for your brother.”
Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. Whenever he went in to his brother’s wife, he spilled his semen on the ground so that he would not give offspring to his brother.
He too was evil in the Lord’s sight because he did this, and the Lord killed him too.

Judah said to Tamar, his daughter-in-law, “Remain a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up.” For he said, “Perhaps this one too will die like his brothers.” So Tamar went and lived in her father’s house.
When her days came to an end, Shua, Judah’s wife, died. After Judah’s grief had subsided, he went up to Timnah, where his sheep were being shorn, together with Hirah, his Adullamite shepherd.
They informed Tamar, their daughter-in-law, saying to her, “Look, your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.”
She took off her widow’s clothes, put on her veil, got up, and sat at a gateway on the road to Timnah. For she saw that Shelah had grown up, but Judah was unwilling to give her to him as his wife.
When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, because she had covered her face, and he did not recognize her.
He turned aside from the road toward her and said, “Let me sleep with you.” She said to him, “What will you give me if you sleep with me?”
He said to her, “I will send you a young goat from our flock.” She said to him, “Give me a pledge until you send it to me.”
He said to her, “What shall I give you as a pledge?” She said to him, “Your signet ring, your head covering, and the staff in your hand.” He gave them to her and slept with her, and she conceived.
She got up and went away, took off those clothes, and put on her widow’s clothes.
Judah sent her the young goat by his Adullamite shepherd, so that he could recover his pledge from the woman, but he did not find her.
He asked the people of that place, “Where is the prostitute who was sitting by the road?” They said to him, “There is no prostitute here.”
He returned to Judah and said to him, “I did not find her, and the people of that place also told me, ‘There is no prostitute here.’”
Judah said, “Let her keep it, so that they do not laugh at us. I did send the young goat, and since you did not find her, let it be.”
Then, after three months, they informed Judah, saying, “Your daughter-in-law Tamar has acted as a prostitute, and now she is pregnant through prostitution.” Judah said, “Bring her out and burn her.”

As they were taking her away, she sent word to her father-in-law, saying, “Whose is this, and which man is responsible for this pregnancy? [?]” And she said to him, “Look at this head covering and this staff.”
Judah saw this and said, “Tamar is more righteous than I am, because I did not give her my son Shelah.” (Then he gave up putting her to death.) Judah did not sleep with her again.
When she gave birth, there were twins in her womb.
Then, as she was giving birth, one put out his hand, and the midwife took it and tied a scarlet thread around his hand, saying, “This one came out first.”
When he drew back his hand, his brother came out, and she said, “This is amazing!” She named him Perez.
After him, his brother also came out, the one who had [?] on his hand, and she named him Zerah.
Joseph went down to the land of Egypt, and Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch and chief cook, an Egyptian man, bought him. He took him from the Ishmaelites, from those who had brought him down there.
The Lord was with Joseph, and he became a blessed man and was put in charge of his master’s household.
When his master saw that the Lord was with him and that the Lord made everything he did succeed through his hands,
Joseph found favor with his master because he pleased him. His master put him in charge of his whole household and entrusted and handed over everything he had to Joseph.

Then, after he was put in charge of the whole household, the Lord blessed that Egyptian because of Joseph. The Lord’s blessing was upon him and all his possessions, both in the fields and in the town.
He placed everything he had in Joseph’s hands. He himself knew nothing about his possessions except the food he ate. Joseph was handsome, and his face was very attractive.
After this, his master’s wife set her eyes on Joseph and said to him, “Sleep with me.”
But he refused her and said, “My master has placed everything he has in my hands, and he knows nothing at all about what is in his house.
There is nothing in this house that has not been entrusted to me except you, because you are his wife. How, then, could I do this evil thing?”
She spoke to Joseph every morning, but he refused to sleep with her or approach her.
One day Joseph went into the house to do his work, and there was no one inside the house.
She grabbed his clothing and said to him, “Come, sleep with me.” But he left his clothes in her hand, fled, and went outside.
When she saw that he had gone out and left his garment in her hand,

She called to those who were in the house and said to them, “What have you brought upon me? (Look at what he did to me!) A Hebrew slave, to mock me! He came to me and said, ‘Sleep with me,’ and I cried out loudly.”
“When he heard that I raised my voice and cried out, he left his garment and fled outside.”
she kept his garment with her until his master came home.
She told him this story and said to him, “Your Hebrew slave, whom you brought among us to mock us, came to me (and said to me). ‘Let me sleep with you,’ he said to me.”
“When he heard that I raised my voice and cried out, he left his garment and fled outside.”
When his master heard his wife’s account, as she told him, “This is what your Hebrew slave did to me,” he became very angry.
He took Joseph and put him in prison, where the king’s prisoners were held in confinement.
The Lord was with Joseph and poured out his mercy upon him, and gave him favor with the chief prison guard.
He entrusted the whole prison to Joseph.

The chief prison guard knew nothing at all about everything being done in the prison, because he had left everything to Joseph. The Lord was with him, and the Lord made everything he did succeed through his hands.
After this, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker offended their master, the king of Egypt.
The chief of his eunuchs became angry with both of them.
The chief jailer put them in prison, in the place where Joseph was, and kept them in confinement.
Both of them dreamed on the same night. Each had his own dream—the chief cupbearer and the chief baker of the king of Egypt, who were in prison.
Joseph came to them and saw that they were troubled.
Joseph questioned them, saying, “Why do your faces look sad today?”
They said to him, “We have dreamed a dream, but we have no one to interpret it for us.” Joseph said to them, “Is it not the person to whom God grants it who interprets dreams? Now tell me.”
The chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream and said to him, “In my dream I saw a vine before me.
On that vine three branches sprouted, and it produced a cluster of grapes.
Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand. I took that cluster and squeezed it into Pharaoh’s cup, and I handed it to him.”
Joseph said to him, “This is its interpretation: these three clusters are three days.

Within three days Pharaoh will remember your position and restore you as chief cupbearer. You will hand Pharaoh his cup with your own hand, as you did in your former position when you were among the cupbearers.
Remember me when things go well for you, and show me kindness. Speak to Pharaoh about me and get me out of prison.
For I was secretly kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews, and here too they put me in prison although I had done nothing.”
When the chief baker saw that Joseph had interpreted the dream correctly for him, he said to Joseph, “I too saw something like this. In my dream I saw three baskets on my head.
In those three baskets, on top, was every kind of food that Pharaoh, king of Egypt, eats, and the birds ate it from the basket on my head.”
Joseph answered him, “This is the interpretation of your dream: these three baskets are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will cut off your head and hang you on a tree, and the birds of the sky will eat your flesh off you.”
On the third day, Pharaoh’s birthday, he held a feast for his people. Among the people he remembered the position of the chief cupbearer and the position of the chief baker.
He restored the chief cupbearer to his position, and he placed the cup in Pharaoh’s hand.
But he hanged the chief baker on a tree, just as Joseph had interpreted for him.
The chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.
After two years Pharaoh had a dream like this: he was standing beside the river.
Seven cows came up out of the river, fine-looking and fat, and grazed on the riverbank.
Another seven cows came up after them, ugly-looking and thin, and grazed beside those cows on the riverbank.
Those seven ugly-looking, thin cows swallowed the cows that were fat and fine-looking. Then Pharaoh woke up.
He dreamed again, and there were seven choice, fine heads of grain growing from one stalk.
And there were seven thin, wind-blasted heads of grain, which came up with them.
And those seven thin, wind-blasted heads of grain swallowed those seven choice, full heads of grain. Then Pharaoh woke up and realized that he had been dreaming.
When morning came, his spirit was troubled, and he sent for all the interpreters of Egypt and all their wise men. He told them his dream, but they could not interpret it for Pharaoh.
Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, “Today I remember my sins, my lord Pharaoh.
Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put us in prison, me and the chief baker.
We both dreamed a dream, he and I; each of us dreamed his own dream.
There was a young Hebrew man with us who belonged to the chief cook. We told him, and he interpreted our dreams for us.
And it happened to us just as he had interpreted for us; that was what we experienced. I returned to my office, and they hanged the other man.”
Then Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and they summoned him. They brought him out of prison, shaved him, changed his clothes, and brought him to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I dreamed a dream, but I could find no one to interpret it for me. I have heard about you that you hear a dream and interpret it.”
Joseph answered Pharaoh and said to him, “No one can interpret this unless God grants it to him.”
Pharaoh told Joseph, saying, “In my dream I saw myself standing on the bank of the river.
Seven cows came up out of the river, from the riverbank, fat in body and beautiful in appearance, and they grazed in the meadow.
And there were seven other cows coming up after them out of the river, bad and ugly in appearance and thin in flesh. I had never seen any as ugly as these in all the land of Egypt.
Those lean cows swallowed those seven fat and beautiful cows.
They went into their bellies, but it was as though nothing had gone into their bellies, and their appearance was as ugly as before. Then I woke up and went to sleep again.
And in a dream I saw seven heads of grain coming up on one stalk, full and good.
And seven other heads of grain, thin and dried up, came up from among them.
Those thin, dried-up heads swallowed the full, good heads. I told the interpreters, but there was no one who interpreted it for me.”
Joseph said to Pharaoh, “Pharaoh’s dream is one. God has shown Pharaoh what he is going to do.”
“The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good heads of grain are seven years. Pharaoh’s dream is one.
The seven thin cows that came up after them are seven years, and the seven thin, wind-blasted heads of grain are seven years. There will be seven years of famine.
This is what I told Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what he is going to do.
Seven years of great abundance are coming throughout the land of Egypt.
Seven years of famine will come afterward, and they will forget the abundance throughout the land of Egypt.
The whole land will perish from hunger because of that famine which is coming afterward, for it will be very severe.
Pharaoh’s dream was repeated because the matter is firmly established by God, and God will bring it about quickly.
Now, find yourself a wise and discerning man and appoint him over all the land of Egypt.”
“Let Pharaoh build storehouses throughout the land of Egypt, and let them seal up Egypt’s grain from the seven years.”
Let them gather all the grain from the seven years of plenty, and let Pharaoh gather his wheat and grain in the cities and keep it safe.
Let the grain they store be food for the whole land during the famine that will come upon the land of Egypt, so that the people do not die of hunger.
This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his people.
Pharaoh said to all his people, “Can anyone be found like this man, upon whom the Spirit of God rests?”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Since God has shown you all this, there is no man wiser or more discerning than you.
You shall be over my entire household, and all the people shall obey your word. Only in regard to the throne shall I be greater than you.”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Look, I appoint you over the whole land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh took his ring from his hand and put it on Joseph’s hand. He clothed him in linen garments and placed a gold necklace around his neck.
He had him ride on his own horse, and a herald went before him making proclamations. He appointed him over the whole land of Egypt.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I myself am Pharaoh, but without you I will do nothing in the whole land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah, and he gave him Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of the city of Heliopolis, to be his wife.
Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. After Joseph left Pharaoh’s presence, he traveled throughout the whole land of Egypt.
And all the grain that the land produced during the seven years of plenty [?].
They gathered all the grain of the land of Egypt and stored grain in all the cities and districts of the land to serve as food.
Joseph stored wheat in enormous quantities, like the sand of the sea, until they could no longer count it. It became beyond counting.
Before the days of famine came, two sons were born to Joseph, whom Asenath bore to him.
He named his firstborn Manasseh, saying, “God has made me forget all my suffering and everything belonging to my father’s household.”
He named the second Ephraim, saying, “God has made me prosper in the land of suffering.”
After the seven years of plenty had passed,
the seven years of famine began to come, just as Joseph had said.
There was famine throughout the land of Egypt, and all the people cried out to Pharaoh for food. He said to them, “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.”
The famine spread over the whole face of the earth. When Joseph saw it, he opened the grain storehouses and sold grain to all the people of Egypt.
Everyone came in caravans to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, because the famine had become severe throughout the whole land.
Jacob heard that there was grain for sale in the land of Egypt, and he said to his sons, “Why are you distressed?
Look, I have heard that there is grain in the land of Egypt. Go, then, and buy some for us, so that we may live and not die of hunger.”
Joseph’s ten brothers went down to buy grain in the land of Egypt.
But he did not send Benjamin, Joseph’s brother, with his brothers, because he said, “He too must not come to harm.”
The sons of Israel came to Joseph because there was a severe famine in the land of Canaan.
Joseph was the governor of Egypt, and he sold grain to all the peoples of the earth. When Joseph’s brothers came, they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground.
When Joseph saw his brothers, he recognized them and spoke harshly to them. He said to them, “Where have you come from?” They said to him, “From the land of Canaan, to buy grain.”
Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.
Joseph remembered the dream he had dreamed and said to them, “You are spies! You have come to see the land’s weaknesses.”
They said to him, “No, my lord! Your servants have come to buy grain.”
“We are all sons of one man. Your servants are not spies.”
He said to them, “No! You are spies, and you have come to discover the unprotected parts of the land.”
They said to him, “We, your servants, are twelve brothers from the land of Canaan. One, the youngest, is with our father, and another has died.”
He said to them, “That is why I tell you: you are spies!”
“This is how you will be tested: as surely as Pharaoh lives, you will not leave here unless you bring your youngest brother.”
“Send one of you to bring your brother, while the rest of you remain until your story is tested to see whether you are telling the truth. Otherwise, as surely as Pharaoh lives, you are spies!”
He put them in prison for three days.
He said to them, “Do this and live, for I fear God.”
But if you are honest, let one of you remain in prison, while the rest of you go and take the grain you have bought.
“Bring your youngest brother to me, and we will believe what you say. Otherwise, you will die.” And they did so.

And they said to one another, “Truly, this has happened to us because of our sin, for we ignored our brother’s suffering when he pleaded with us for mercy, and we did not listen to him then. That is why this suffering has come upon us.”
And [?] answered them and said, “Did I not tell you, ‘Do not wrong the boy’? But you did not listen to me. Now, today, you are being called to account for his blood.”
They did not know that Joseph understood them, because there was an interpreter between them.
Joseph turned away from them and wept. Then he returned to them and spoke to them. He took Simeon and bound him before their eyes.
Joseph ordered that their sacks be brought and grain put in them, and that each man’s gold also be put in his sack. They did everything as he ordered.
They loaded their grain onto their donkeys and left that place.
One of them opened his sack at the place where they spent the night to take out feed for their donkeys. He found his bundle of gold in the mouth of his sack.

He said to them, “My gold has been returned to me! Look, I found it in the mouth of my sack.” Their hearts sank, and they trembled among themselves, saying, “What has God done to us? What is this that has happened?”
They reached their father Jacob in the land of Canaan and told him everything that had happened to them.
They said to him, “The man who rules the land spoke harshly to us and put us in prison as though we were spying on the land.”
“We told him, ‘We are honest men, not spies.’”
“‘We are twelve brothers, sons of one man. One of us has died, and the youngest is with our father in the land of Canaan.’”
“The man who rules the land said to us, ‘This is how you will be shown to be honest: leave one of your brothers here with me, take the grain you have bought, and go.’”
Bring your brother to me, and I will know that you are trustworthy and are not spies. Then I will return your brother to you, and you may trade in our land.
Then, when they emptied their sacks, they found all their bundles of gold in their sacks. When they saw their gold, both they and their father were afraid.
Jacob said to them, “You have deprived me of my children. Joseph is gone, and Simeon is gone, and you are taking Benjamin from me. Has all this come upon me?”
Reuben said to his father, “Kill both my sons if I do not bring him back to you. Entrust him to my care, and I will bring him back to you.”

He said to them, “My son will not go down with you, because his brother has died and he alone is left. If he should fall ill on the road as you travel, you will bring my gray hair down to the grave in sorrow.”
After this, the famine became severe in the land.
When they had finished eating the grain they had brought from the land of Egypt, their father said to them, “Go again and buy a little grain to bring us.”
Judah said to him, “The man who rules the land solemnly warned us, saying, ‘You will not see my face unless your younger brother comes with you.’
“If you send our brother with us, we will go and buy grain for you.
But if you do not send our brother with us, we will not go, because the man told us, ‘You will not see my face unless you bring your younger brother with you.’”
And Israel said to them, “Why have you done this evil to me by telling that man that you have another brother?”

They said to him, “The man asked about our family, saying, ‘Is your father, the old man, still alive? Do you have a brother?’ We answered him according to what he asked us. Could we have known that he would tell us, ‘Bring your brother’?”
Judah said to his father, “Send the boy with me, and let us get up and go, so that we and our livestock may live and not die.
I will be responsible for him; hold me accountable. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, I will bear the guilt before you all my life.
If we had not delayed, we could already have returned a second time.”

Their father Israel said to them, “If that is how matters stand, take some of the produce of the land, put it in your sacks, and take it to the man as a gift: resin, honey, incense, storax, pistachios, and walnuts.
Take twice as much gold with you, and also take back the gold you found inside your sacks and brought away unknowingly; perhaps it was a mistake.
Take your brother with you too, and get up and go down to the man.
May my God grant you favor with the man, so that he sends back your other brother and Benjamin. As for me, if I am deprived of my children, I am deprived.”
The men took that gift, and they took twice as much gold with them, along with Benjamin. They set out and went down to the land of Egypt and came before Joseph.

Joseph saw Benjamin with them and said to the steward of his house, “Bring these people into the house. Slaughter an animal and prepare it, because these men will dine with me and eat the midday meal with me.”
And the man did as Joseph told him and brought the men into Joseph’s house.

When the men saw that they were being brought into Joseph’s house, they said, “They are taking us in because of the gold that was returned in our sacks the first time, so that they can condemn us, make us slaves, and take our livestock.”
They approached the man in charge of Joseph’s house and spoke to him at the doorway of the house.
And they said to him, “Please, my lord, we came down before to buy grain.”
“When we reached our lodging place and opened our sacks, we found our gold inside our sacks, each man’s own gold. Now we have brought our gold back with us, each amount at its full weight.
We have also brought other gold with us to buy grain. We do not know who put that gold in our sacks.”

The man said to them, “Be at ease; do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your fathers has given you treasure in your sacks. As for your money, I willingly received it.” He also brought Simeon out to them.
He brought water for their feet and gave food to their donkeys.
And they prepared their gift for Joseph’s arrival at noon, for they had heard that he would eat there.
When Joseph came into his house, they brought him his gift from what they had in their house, and bowed before him with their faces to the ground.
He asked them how they were and said to them, “Is your father well—that old man whom you told me was still alive?”
And they said to him, “Your servant, our elderly father, is well, and he is still alive.” And Joseph said, “That man is blessed by God.” And they lowered their heads and bowed down to him.

When he looked and saw Benjamin, his brother, his mother's son, he said to them, “Is this your younger brother, whom you said you would bring to me?” They said to him, “Yes.” Joseph said to him, “May the Lord be gracious to you, my son.”
Joseph was deeply moved and wanted to weep. He went into an inner room and wept.
He washed his face and came out, controlling himself, and said, “Bring us bread.”
They served them separately, and him separately, and the Egyptians who were dining separately. For the Egyptians could not eat food with the Hebrews, because the Egyptians despised all shepherds.
Their eldest, the firstborn, sat before him, and the younger ones according to their ages. They looked at one another in amazement.
And they received their portions from him, each his own. Benjamin’s portion was five times greater than any of theirs. And they drank and became drunk with him.
Joseph commanded his steward, saying to him, “Fill these men's sacks with as much as they can carry, and put each one's money in his sack.
Put my silver cup in the youngest one's sack, and put in the money for his food as well.” He did as Joseph had told him.
When morning dawned, he sent the men away with their animals.

When the men had gone out, before they had gone far from the city, Joseph said to the steward of his house, “Get up, pursue these men and follow them. Catch up with them and say to them, ‘Why do you repay me with evil in return for good?
Why have you stolen from me the silver cup from which my master drinks? You have done evil.’ Tell them this.”
He went and found them and said to them, “Why do you do this, repaying me with evil in return for the good I did for you, and stealing my master's silver cup from me?”
They said to him, “Why do you speak like this, our lord? Far be it from your servants! They would not do such a thing.
We brought back to you from the land of Canaan the large amount of money that we found in our sacks. How, then, could we steal gold or silver from your house?
Now, whichever of us, your servants, you find your cup with, let him die, and we will become slaves to your master.”
He said to them, “Now let it be as you have said: the one with whom the cup is found will become our slave, but you have cleared yourselves.”
They quickly lowered their sacks to the ground and began opening them,
from the oldest to the youngest, and he found the cup in Benjamin's sack.
They tore their clothes, loaded their sacks onto their donkeys, and returned to the city.
[And they entered Joseph’s house] while he was still [there], and they fell facedown on the ground.
And Joseph said to them, “What is this you have done?”

Judah said, “What can we answer our lord? What can we say? How can we clear ourselves, since God has brought our wrongdoing back upon us? Look, we have become slaves to our lord, both we and this man with whom the cup was found.”
Joseph said, “Far be it from me to do such a thing! The man with whom my cup was found will be my slave. But you, go to your father in peace.”
Judah approached him and said, “Please, my lord, allow me to speak before you, my lord. Do not be angry with your servant, for you are next after Pharaoh.”
My lord, you asked your servants, saying, “Do you have a father or a brother?”
We told you, my lord, “We have an elderly father, and he has a young son born in his old age. His brother is dead, and he alone remains of his mother’s children, and his father loves him.”
You said to your servants, “Bring him to me, and I will look after him.”
We told you, “The child cannot leave his father. If he leaves him, he will die.”
But you said to your servants, “Unless you bring your younger brother, you will not see my face again.”
And when we went up to your servant, our father, we told him what you had said to us, my lord.
Our father said to us, “Go again and buy us a little food.”
We told him, “We cannot go unless our younger brother comes with us, for we cannot see that man’s face unless our younger brother is with us.”
And your servant, our father, said to us, “You yourselves know that this woman bore me two sons.”
“One went away from me, and you told me, ‘A wild animal ate him.’ And I have [?] seen him again to this day.”
“If you take this one too away from me, and he happens to fall ill on the journey, you will bring my gray head down to the grave in sorrow.”
“And now, if we go to your servant, our father, and this boy is not with us—for his life is bound to this boy—
